description: Team from Kyiv working on Lunar Landing Site Navigator: a simple tool to compare lunar south pole landing sites and dates by sunlight, solar power and Earth visibility for direct communication, built on NASA LOLA terrain and SPICE ephemerides and checked against JPL Horizons. On board: backend and data (Python), physics and astronomy, React front end, 3D (Blender, three.js).
summary: Lunar Navigator is a free website that helps mission planners, students and anyone curious choose a landing site and a date at the lunar south pole. For 10 candidate sites, or any point you click, it shows how much of the time the site is in sunlight (power), how long the longest darkness lasts (batteries), when Earth is above the horizon (direct radio link) and how many hours remain until the next sunset and Earthset. Real mountains on the horizon are taken into account, because at the pole the Sun never climbs more than a few degrees. Everything is computed from NASA data (NAIF SPICE ephemerides and LRO LOLA terrain) and checked against NASA: Sun and Earth directions match JPL Horizons within 0.00003° over 1,210 positions, the sunlit share matches NASA's LOLA illumination map with a median difference of 0.26 percentage points (correlation 0.996), and 149 of 150 permanently shadowed pixels stay dark. Example: at Connecting ridge a 10 m mast instead of a 1 m panel raises yearly sunlight from 86.5 % to 93.5 % and cuts the longest night from 182 h to 75 h. The site works on a phone and a laptop without an account.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Navigator answers two questions every south pole mission asks: when will this site have sunlight for power, and when can it talk to Earth directly? It has seven sheets:

- 00 Globe: the whole Moon from a compressed LRO model with the ten sites on it; pick a site on the globe and open the view from the ground.

- 01 Map: the south pole from 83° S to 90° S on NASA's average illumination map, 10 candidate sites, a card for the chosen site, and a "Now" layer that shows light and shadow over the whole pole at the chosen hour. Click anywhere to compute your own point in the browser.

- 02 Compare: sites side by side for any period (for example the darkest 30 days or a mission window): sunlit share, longest darkness, longest continuous light, highest Sun, sunlight on a panel facing the Sun, Earth in view, hours to the first sunset and Earthset. The best value in each row is marked.

- 03 Timeline: elevation of the Sun and the Earth against the real terrain in their directions, hour by hour, with strips of "Sun visible" and "Earth in view".

- 04 Horizon: a live 3D scene from LOLA terrain at eye level or from above. The terrain casts real shadows that move with the time slider. The Sun and Earth are drawn in their true directions and sizes, with an elevation scale. The whole 360° horizon is also unrolled as a panorama with the paths of the Sun and the Earth. At night the page says so and offers a jump to sunrise.

- 05 Why: five ideas in pictures for students: the Sun never climbs, mountains decide who gets light, a few metres of mast change everything, Earth hangs low and wobbles, panels stand upright.

- 06 Accuracy: how the numbers were checked against NASA sources, and where the model stops.

On the Timeline and Horizon sheets the instrument height can be set to 1, 2, 5 or 10 m, and Compare has a whole-year table for all four heights: a mast of a few metres can turn days of darkness into hours.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Sun and Earth: positions from NAIF SPICE kernels (DE440 planetary ephemeris, Moon orientation in the MOON_ME frame), with light time and aberration, every hour for a year from 14 Nov 2026.

2. Horizon: for each site the elevation angle of the terrain in 720 directions out to 150 km, from LOLA elevation models (5 m site models near the site, 20 m, 80 m and 120 m polar models further out), with the curvature of the Moon.

3. Metrics: the visible part of the solar disc over the horizon, the same rule NASA's illumination maps use (the Sun counts as visible while any part of its disc is above the terrain). From it come the sunlit share, darkness, Earth windows, and the next sunset and Earthset.

4. Website: precomputed results are static files on GitHub Pages, so the site never sleeps. Any period is summarised in the browser. Your own points and the Now layer are computed in the browser from a 240 m elevation grid and hourly Sun directions. The 3D shadows are traced over the site's 20 m terrain tile, with the far hills taken from the site's horizon.

CAN YOU TRUST THE NUMBERS

- Sun and Earth directions against JPL Horizons: 1,210 positions, largest difference 0.00003° (target was 0.01°).

- Sunlit share against NASA's LOLA illumination map, recomputed the way the map was made (60 m model, 18.6 years) at 480 random pixels: median difference 0.26 percentage points, correlation 0.996.

- Permanently shadowed regions of the NASA map: 149 of 150 pixels never lit in our computation.

- Period summaries made in the browser reproduce the backend's yearly numbers for all 10 sites (automatic test).

- Your own points use a coarser 240 m grid: at 480 test pixels the median difference from the full computation is 0.4 percentage points, nine in ten are within 5.7 points, and sharp peaks can differ more. The page says so.

Details: the Accuracy sheet and docs/VALIDATION.md in the repository.

BENEFITS

Existing tools such as JPL Horizons, Moon Trek and Quickmap are made for experts. Lunar Navigator puts the answer for a site and a date on one screen, explains it in plain words and pictures, shows how far to trust it, and runs on any phone without installation or an account.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE NEXT

Windows for relay satellites when Earth is hidden, more sites from the published Artemis regions, and finer terrain for the points users choose themselves.

TOOLS

Python (spiceypy, numpy, numba, rasterio, pyproj, FastAPI, pytest) for the computation and validation. TypeScript, React, three.js with React Three Fiber, Recharts, Vite and Vitest for the website, with Web Workers for the in-browser computation. GitHub and GitHub Pages for code and hosting. No special hardware.

Open source under Apache-2.0.

LINKS

Website: https://evge14n.github.io/spaceu-lunar-navigator/

Code: https://github.com/Evge14n/spaceu-lunar-navigator

Seven-slide overview (PDF): https://evge14n.github.io/spaceu-lunar-navigator/slides/demo.pdf

Video demo (30 s): https://youtu.be/v6LDgqZ6jKI

SITES

The 10 sites are the south pole landing-site areas of the NASA PGDA LOLA 5 m/pixel set (Barker et al. 2021): Connecting ridge, Shackleton rim, Nobile rim 1 and 2, Peak near Shackleton, de Gerlache rim, Leibnitz beta plateau, Malapert massif, Haworth and Shoemaker. Any other point can be computed in the browser.

WHAT ONLY THIS TOOL SHOWS

Instrument height of 1, 2, 5 or 10 m with a whole-year table (at Connecting ridge a 10 m mast raises yearly sunlight from 86.5 % to 93.5 % and cuts the longest night from 182 h to 75 h), a light-and-shadow layer over the whole pole for any hour, and any point computed in the browser.

LIMITATIONS

- "Earth in view" is geometric line of sight; Deep Space Network schedules and a radio link budget are not included yet.

- Sunlight assumes an ideal panel; there is no battery or power model yet.

- Your own points use the 240 m grid; the 10 sites use 5-20 m terrain.

- Timelines cover one year from 14 Nov 2026.

- Next: DSN contact windows, CSV/PDF export, more sites (Artemis III regions, CLPS), comparison with real mission landings.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE

Claude helped with the code.
